threads.thread_goal: Align on current issues and approve target workflow scope

messages.text:
Kicking off the front-of-house standardisation work for project_pack_ref: Standardising Pharmacy Front-of-House Workflow and Stock Layout.
I have started mapping the current steps for prescriptions and OTC requests for T1 and will draft them into A1 so we can all react.
To get this right, can everyone share the main pain points you see from customer arrival to medication handover? Also, which processes do you think must be in scope for the new standard workflow (for example: receiving prescriptions, OTC advice, handover, payment, and any stock-related steps at the counter)?
Once we have a list, we can agree what is in or out and then rank the top issues to tackle first.

From my shifts, the biggest issues are:
- When it is busy, we sometimes mix up who is handling which prescription, especially if the customer steps away and comes back.
- OTC requests can block the queue when we have to leave the counter to check shelves.
- At handover, we are not always consistent in what we explain to the customer.
For scope, I think we should include: greeting and first question, checking prescription or OTC need, preparing the medication, double-checking, taking payment, and documenting anything unusual.

Adding what I see:
- We do not always follow the same order when we get a prescription, sometimes we label first, sometimes we pick first.
- When stock is missing, each of us handles it differently with the customer.
- For OTC, we sometimes give advice at the till and sometimes we move to the side counter, which confuses people.
I agree those steps should be in scope. Maybe also include how we pass things to the pharmacist when needed.

From the stock side at the front, I notice:
- We sometimes have to walk back and forth because items are not where we expect, which slows down serving.
- When we pull items from the shelf for a prescription, they are not always scanned or noted the same way.
I think the workflow should also cover how we request help from shelf fillers during busy times and how we handle items that need to go back to the shelf if the sale does not go ahead.

One more pain point: when we get multiple family members at once, we sometimes mix up who has paid and who is still waiting for counselling.
Also, near closing time, we rush to finish prescriptions and the steps are not always the same as during the day.
For scope, could we include a short closing routine for the front desk, like final checks and how to park unfinished prescriptions?

From my side, I see:
- Different ways of checking customer identity before handing over medicines.
- Not everyone documents phone advice the same way when the customer later comes in to collect.
Maybe the new workflow should also cover how we record those interactions so it is consistent.

Thanks all, this is helpful. I will start drafting the current-state map for T1 in A1 with these steps:
1) Customer arrival and greeting.
2) Triage: prescription vs OTC vs both.
3) For prescriptions: intake, identity check, data entry, picking, labelling, pharmacist check where needed, handover, counselling, payment.
4) For OTC: brief assessment, product selection, pharmacist involvement when required, handover, payment.
5) Exceptions: missing stock, family groups, phone advice, items to return to shelf, closing-time handling.
Before we lock the scope, are we missing any front-of-house processes that happen regularly at the counter?
Maybe add how we handle emergency situations at the counter, like when someone feels unwell while waiting. Even if it is short, a standard step list would help.
Agree with adding emergencies. Also, what about how we manage queues when there is only one person at the counter versus two? Not sure if that is part of the workflow or more of a rota thing.

For the stock-related parts, could we make sure the workflow shows clearly when we should call a shelf filler instead of leaving the counter? That will help us plan T2 and T6 later so the layout supports the flow.
For the queue management, maybe we can just note the main options, like one till open vs two, and who focuses on prescriptions vs OTC. We can keep it simple so it does not become a rota document.
I think the list you have plus emergencies and basic queue handling covers what I see day to day. Maybe we can keep anything back-office, like ordering stock, out of this scope for now.

Ok, summarising the processes to include in the standard workflow:
- Customer arrival and greeting.
- Triage: prescription, OTC, or both.
- Prescription flow: intake, identity check, data entry, picking, labelling, pharmacist check where needed, handover, counselling, payment.
- OTC flow: brief assessment, product selection, pharmacist involvement when required, handover, payment.
- Exceptions: missing stock, family groups, phone advice linked to later collection, items to return to shelf, closing-time handling.
- Support steps: when to involve shelf fillers, basic queue handling, and short emergency response steps at the counter.
If no one objects, I will record this as the scope for D1 in A1 and move on to ranking the main pain points.
Works for me. No extra processes from my side.
Happy with that scope, especially that it calls out when to involve shelf fillers.
Looks complete to me as well.
All good from my side.

Next, can we agree on the top three pain points to address first in the new workflow? From what you shared, I see candidates:
1) Inconsistent handling of prescriptions and risk of mix-ups when it is busy.
2) OTC requests blocking the queue and needing us to leave the counter.
3) Inconsistent handover and counselling at the till.
Other issues like closing-time rush and documentation of phone advice are important, but maybe we can treat them as second wave.
Please react or suggest changes so we can confirm D2.
I agree with those three. If we fix them, it should already improve safety and the queue a lot.
Same here, those are the ones I struggle with most on busy days.
From the stock side, point 2 is key. If we design the layout and support steps around that, it will help a lot.
I am ok with those three as the first focus. We can still add closing-time routines later in the same document.
Agree with the list and the order.

Thanks all. I will record D2 as:
Top three pain points to address first in the new workflow are:
1) Inconsistent handling of prescriptions and risk of mix-ups.
2) OTC requests blocking the queue and requiring us to leave the counter.
3) Inconsistent handover and counselling at the till.
I will reflect this in the next version of A1 and the mapping for T1 so we design the future workflow around these.

threads.thread_goal: Define and approve the standard shelf layout and labelling rules

messages.text:
I have put together a first draft of the standard shelf layout map in A2 for T2, focusing on the pain points we listed earlier.
Key ideas:
- Clear separation between prescription-only stock behind the counter and OTC in front.
- High-risk medicines grouped in a dedicated, clearly marked section behind the counter.
- Fast-moving OTC categories placed near the counter to reduce walking.
Before we move to a pilot for T6, can the assistants look at A2 and comment on whether the flow from the counter makes sense?

Looking at A2 now. First impression: the separation between high-risk and regular prescription stock is clear, which is good for safety.
One question: for temperature-sensitive items that we keep in the fridge, how do you see them represented in the map so it links with T11 and the labelling rules in A3?

From the counter view, I like that cough and cold products are closer. That should help with OTC queues.
I am a bit unsure about the vitamins being split across two bays. Would it be better to keep them together so we do not have to remember two spots?
I agree with keeping high-risk medicines in one marked area. Could we also mark the shelves for look-alike, sound-alike medicines more clearly? That might need a rule in A3 so we are consistent.
The OTC pain relief section looks a bit tight in the draft. On busy days we reach for those a lot. Could we widen that area or move some less-used items further away?

Good point on temperature-sensitive items. For T11, I suggest we:
- Show the fridge as a separate block on A2, with clear categories inside.
- Use a specific colour or symbol on the map and on labels for fridge items, defined in A3.
That way, the layout, the storage practice, and the labelling rules all match. Does that work from your side at the counter?

On vitamins: I split them because of space, but we can group them in one bay by moving some low-demand items to the top shelf or to a side bay.
If that helps you pick faster and avoid errors, I can adjust A2 before we pilot T6.

For pain relief, we can widen that section by reducing the space for seasonal items. They move less outside peak season.
I will update the draft so pain relief has a full bay near the counter.

Yes, having the fridge as a separate block with a symbol for temperature-sensitive items will help a lot. It will also make it easier to check we follow the storage rules when we review T11.
On the high-risk area, could we add a rule that those shelves must not be used for anything else, even temporarily? That might sit in A3 as well.
Agree on keeping the high-risk area exclusive. Maybe we can also add a small visual cue on the shelf labels, like a coloured strip, so we notice quickly if something is in the wrong place.

Looking at the OTC side, I like that first-aid items are grouped. Could we also keep all thermometers and blood pressure devices together near the health advice area? Customers often ask questions about them, and it would be easier if they are in one place.

For A3, I propose these basic labelling rules for high-risk and temperature-sensitive medicines:
- High-risk: shelf labels with a coloured strip and a clear note, and products stored only in the dedicated high-risk area.
- Temperature-sensitive: fridge symbol on both product labels and shelf labels, and items only in the fridge block on A2.
We will still need pharmacist or health and safety sign-off, but does this cover what you need at the counter?
From my side, those rules are clear and easy to follow. We just need to make sure they align with the storage and labelling regulations when we ask the pharmacist to review A3 and T11.
I understand the coloured strip and fridge symbol. That will help me spot items quickly. No extra changes from me.
Same here, the rules sound straightforward. As long as we get a short guide to remind us which colour means what, I am fine.

Based on your feedback, I will update A2 to:
- Group vitamins in one bay.
- Widen the pain relief section near the counter.
- Show the fridge as a separate block with a symbol for temperature-sensitive items.
- Keep high-risk medicines in a dedicated, clearly marked area.
Unless there are strong objections, can we treat this updated A2 as the initial standard layout for the pilot section in T6 and record that as D3?
I am happy to go ahead with that layout for the pilot.
Ok for me as well. We can fine-tune after we see how it works in practice.
Yes, let us test it in one section first.
Fine by me.

To close the loop on labelling rules: we have agreed that high-risk shelves will have a coloured strip and be used only for those medicines, and temperature-sensitive items will have a fridge symbol on product and shelf labels and be stored only in the fridge block.
I will document this in A3 and link it to T4 and T11, then ask the pharmacist or health and safety officer to review.
I will record this agreement as D4.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in SOPs for stock reception and daily checks

messages.text:
I have drafted the steps for receiving and storing new stock for T3 and a first version of the daily shelf and stock verification checklist for T9.
Both are in A1 and A5 for review.
For stock reception (T3), the draft covers: checking deliveries against the order, checking expiry dates and storage conditions, documenting discrepancies, and placing items either in the fridge, high-risk area, or regular shelves according to A2 and A3.
For the daily checklist (T9), A5 lists quick checks per aisle: stock levels, expiry, and label accuracy.
Can you all review and comment on anything missing or unclear before we finalise?

I read the stock reception steps in A1. I understand most of it, but I am not sure when exactly we should involve the pharmacist for discrepancies. Is it only for missing items, or also for short expiry dates?

On the daily checklist in A5, the time estimates per aisle look a bit tight for the bigger sections. For example, two minutes for the full pain relief bay might not be enough if we also check expiry dates.
Maybe we can adjust the times slightly so they are realistic.

From the shelf filler side, I like that A5 separates stock level, expiry, and label accuracy.
One suggestion: can we add a quick note in T9 that if we find a label issue on a high-risk or temperature-sensitive item, we must flag it immediately to the pharmacist or lead assistant, not just note it for later?
For stock reception, could we add a simple step about cleaning the area before and after unpacking, to keep hygiene standards? I did not see that clearly in A1.
On the checklist, I like the structure but I am not sure how often we should do the full expiry check. Is it daily for all aisles, or do we rotate sections?

Good question. For discrepancies in T3, I suggest we:
- Always involve the pharmacist for missing items, wrong items, or damaged stock.
- Involve the pharmacist for short expiry dates if the remaining shelf life is below the threshold in our organisational guideline.
I will add a line in A1 to say we follow the existing guideline and escalate to the pharmacist when in doubt, since we cannot change that rule ourselves.

Agree on adding a cleaning step. I will insert a short step at the start and end of the reception process in A1: clear and clean the unpacking area, and dispose of packaging according to our waste rules.

For expiry checks in A5, my proposal is:
- Daily quick scan for obviously short-dated or expired items in all aisles.
- A more detailed expiry check on a rotating basis, for example one or two aisles per day, so we cover the whole front-of-house each week.
I will add that rotation note into T9 and A5 so it is clear.

I agree that some time estimates are tight. From experience, I would increase the pain relief bay to four minutes and the vitamins bay to three.
If we all think that is manageable, we can update A5 accordingly.
Those times sound more realistic to me. With the rotation you mentioned, it should still fit into the shift.
Thanks, that helps. With that note in A1, I feel more confident about when to ask the pharmacist to review a delivery.
The added cleaning step makes sense. Could we also mention hand hygiene before handling the medicines, just as a reminder?
Yes, I will add a short line about hand hygiene before starting the reception process, in line with our existing hygiene rules.
The daily quick scan plus rotating detailed check sounds clear. Maybe we can add a small tick box in A5 to mark which aisle had the detailed check that day.
Good catch. I will update T9 and A5 so that any label issue on high-risk or temperature-sensitive items must be escalated immediately to the pharmacist or lead assistant, not just logged.
Perfect, that will help us catch serious issues quickly.

To summarise the SOP for receiving and storing new stock in T3:
- Prepare the area: clean surface, hand hygiene, and have the order list ready.
- Check each delivery against the order, including quantities and product names.
- Check expiry dates and storage conditions, and follow organisational rules on short expiry.
- Document any discrepancies and escalate to the pharmacist for missing, wrong, damaged, or short-dated items as per guideline.
- Place items in the correct location according to A2 and A3: fridge, high-risk area, or regular shelves.
- Clear packaging and leave the area clean.
If everyone is comfortable with this, I will record D5 as approval of this SOP and keep A1 updated.
I am ok with those steps.
Looks good to me as well.
Happy with that SOP.
No further comments from me.

For the daily shelf and stock verification checklist in T9, we have now:
- Daily quick scan of all aisles for obvious stock gaps, misplacements, and expired items.
- Rotating detailed expiry check for selected aisles, with a tick box in A5 to record which ones were done.
- Time estimates per aisle adjusted to realistic values.
- Immediate escalation of label issues on high-risk and temperature-sensitive items.
If there are no objections, I will record D6 as approval of this checklist format and keep A5 as our reference.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on training approach and rollout schedule

messages.text:
I have drafted a training checklist for the new workflow and layout for T5 in A4, and a one-page quick-reference guide for customer communication for T7 in A6.
I also sketched an initial implementation schedule in A8 for T10, trying to avoid peak hours.
Proposal:
- Training format: short small-group sessions at the start or end of shifts, plus self-review using A4 and A6.
- Everyone who works at the front desk or on shelves completes the checklist in A4.
- Implementation slots: layout changes and label updates done in low-traffic periods as shown in A8.
Can you review and say if this training approach and schedule are workable before we confirm?
I like the idea of short sessions. For A4, could we add a column for the trainer to sign as well, not just the staff member? That might help the store manager see who delivered which session.

Looking at A6, the key phrases for common queries are helpful. I wonder if we should add a short reminder about privacy when discussing sensitive topics at the counter, like suggesting we move to a quieter spot.
On A8, the proposed times for layout changes look mostly fine, but the Monday late afternoon slot might still be busy for us. Could we move that to early evening or another day?
For the training checklist in A4, should we include a short section on how to handle near-miss incidents, or will that be covered separately in T8?

On the training format, I support small-group sessions plus self-review. We just need to make sure the store manager agrees with the timing in A8 for T10, since we cannot change staffing without their approval.
For who must complete A4, I would say: all pharmacy assistants, all shelf fillers, and any relief staff who work at the front desk.
Good idea. I will add a trainer signature column to A4 so we can track who delivered each session. That should also help when we review with the store manager for T5.
On A6, I can add a short line under privacy to suggest offering a more private space for sensitive topics, and a reminder not to discuss personal health details loudly at the till.
For near-miss handling, T8 will have its own process and template, but I can add a checkbox in A4 to confirm that each person has been shown how to use the near-miss log in A7.

On the Monday slot in A8, we can move that layout work to later in the evening or to Wednesday morning, which is usually quieter.
I will adjust T10 and A8 to reflect that and then ask the store manager to confirm the final schedule.
The added privacy reminder in A6 will be useful, especially for younger staff who are still getting used to these conversations.
Thanks for moving that slot. With the new times, I think the schedule in A8 will be workable for shelf fillers.
For the training sessions, will we have a short role-play or example for using the new workflow at the counter, or just a walkthrough of the documents?

We can include a short role-play in each session, for example one prescription scenario and one OTC scenario, using the phrases from A6 and the steps from A1.
I will add a note in A4 that the trainer should run through at least one example of each.
Adding the near-miss checkbox to A4 is a good idea. That way we know everyone has seen A7 and T8, even if they do not log an incident straight away.

To make it concrete, I suggest we define the training format as:
- 30-minute small-group sessions (2 to 4 people) at the start or end of shifts.
- Each session covers the new workflow steps, layout and labelling rules, and customer communication using A1, A2, A3, and A6.
- Each participant signs A4, and the trainer signs as well.
- Anyone who works at the front desk or on shelves, including relief staff, must complete A4.
If everyone agrees, we can record this as D7.
I am fine with that training format and who needs to complete A4.
Works for shelf fillers as well.
Agreed.
Ok for me too.

On the implementation schedule in T10, after adjusting the Monday slot, the plan in A8 is now:
- Layout and labelling changes done in short blocks during mid-morning and early afternoon on quieter days.
- Some evening slots for bigger moves, avoiding known peak times.
We will still need the store manager to confirm these times, but if you are all ok with this pattern, we can record D8 as approval of the schedule from our side, pending their sign-off.
The updated schedule works for me, as long as the store manager confirms the staffing.
I am ok with that schedule too.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, near-miss logs, and finalise follow-ups

messages.text:
We have now run the pilot layout in one section for T6 and started using the near-miss log in A7.
I have added a short summary of pilot feedback and incidents into A1 and A2, and drafted the project wrap-up for T12.
Key points so far:
- The new layout reduced walking for common OTC items.
- A few near-miss entries in A7 related to look-alike packs in the pain relief area.
- Some staff still forget to use the daily checklist A5 on busy days.
Can you share your observations from the pilot and any follow-up actions you think we should capture in T8 and T12?

From the shelf side, the pilot layout in A2 worked well overall. We had fewer questions from assistants about where items were.
The near-miss entries in A7 for pain relief were mostly about similar-looking packs being close together. We might need to tweak the micro-layout within that bay, maybe by adding more spacing or clearer shelf labels.

I noticed that with the new layout, I can serve cough and cold requests faster.
On the near-miss side, I had one case where I almost picked the wrong strength of pain relief. I logged it in A7, but I am not sure if I filled all the fields correctly.
I like the new workflow, but I did forget to complete A5 on one very busy afternoon. Maybe we need a small reminder at the end of the shift checklist so we do not skip it.

On customer communication, using A6 helped me keep explanations consistent. I had one near-miss where I almost handed over the wrong OTC product, but I caught it when I repeated the product name back to the customer, as suggested in the guide. I logged it in A7.

From my shifts, the pilot layout reduced back-and-forth walking, but I agree we still have some risk with similar packs.
On T8, I think we should clarify in the near-miss process how quickly we review entries and who leads that review.
On filling A7, if any fields are unclear, we can adjust the instructions in T8 so it is easier to complete. For example, we can add a short example entry at the top of the log.

For the pain relief bay, I can adjust the micro-layout in A2 by:
- Separating similar-looking packs with a different brand or a divider.
- Making sure the shelf labels from A3 highlight the strength clearly.
We can then monitor A7 to see if near-misses in that area drop.

For T8, I suggest we:
- Review A7 entries once a week in a short team huddle.
- Have one assistant prepare a quick summary of patterns before the huddle.
- Note any changes needed to A1, A2, A3, or A5 as follow-up actions.
A reminder at the end of the shift would help me too. Maybe we can add a line in A5 or in our closing routine in A1 to check that the daily checklist has been completed.
I like the idea of a weekly huddle. It will make A7 feel more useful if we see that entries lead to changes in the layout or SOPs.

I can incorporate that into T8: weekly review of A7, one assistant preparing a short summary, and capturing any changes needed to A1, A2, A3, or A5.
We will still need the pharmacist to review any changes that affect safety rules, but we can prepare the suggestions.

Once I update the pain relief bay layout in A2, we should keep an eye on A7 for a couple of weeks to see if the near-miss pattern changes. If not, we might need to consider stronger visual cues or moving some products.
An example entry in A7 would help me a lot. Sometimes I am not sure how much detail to write.
If we add that reminder to A1, maybe we can also mention that if A5 was not completed, we should note the reason and catch up as soon as possible.
Good point. I will add to A1 that at the end of each shift we check whether A5 was completed, and if not, we record why and when it will be done.

For T12, I think the summary should highlight:
- Reduced walking and faster service for common OTC categories.
- Clearer separation of high-risk and temperature-sensitive medicines.
- Use of A5 and A7 to keep shelves accurate and learn from near-misses.
And list follow-up actions like fine-tuning the pain relief bay and reinforcing checklist use.
We could also mention in T12 that the customer communication guide A6 helped standardise how we explain medicines, based on the feedback we heard.

I will update T12 to include:
- The benefits you listed: faster service for key OTC items, clearer separation of high-risk and temperature-sensitive stock, and better use of A5 and A7.
- The impact of A6 on more consistent counselling.
- Remaining follow-ups: adjust the pain relief bay layout, monitor near-miss trends, and reinforce daily checklist completion.
Once I have a clean draft, I will share it with the pharmacist and store manager as the final project summary.
